title: How to Digitize Your Wardrobe and Use an Outfit App
h1: How to digitize your wardrobe, step by step
excerpt: How to digitize your wardrobe in any app: photographing clothes, light and backgrounds, tagging, what to skip, and keeping your digital closet up to date.
tldr: Photograph each piece flat on a plain, contrasting background in daylight, add the photos to a wardrobe app in batches, and tag each item by type, colour, season and formality. Start with the 20 to 30 pieces you wear most, and keep the app current by photographing new clothes before their first wear.
body:
To digitize your wardrobe, photograph each piece flat on a plain background in daylight, add the photos to a wardrobe app, and tag every item with a few basics: type, colour, season and how formal it is. Start with the 20 to 30 things you wear most, not everything you own, and add the rest as they come out of the wash.

The steps below work in any wardrobe app, on any phone. Where an app's own guidance is useful, it's linked so you can check the details yourself. If the idea is new to you, start with what a digital wardrobe is.

Before you start: choose an app and a starting set

Two checks matter more than the feature list. First, does the app run on the device you'll actually use? Some wardrobe apps are iPhone-only, some are Android or web. Second, where do your photos live: on your phone, or on the company's servers? That affects privacy and what happens if you switch phones. Our guide to the downsides and privacy questions of wardrobe apps covers what to look for, the best digital wardrobe apps list compares the main options, and our Whering vs Indyx vs Stylebook comparison sets the three best-known side by side.

Then choose your starting set: the clothes you've worn in the last month or two, plus shoes and one or two coats. Skipping the rest at first isn't laziness. In a 2022 WRAP survey of more than 6,000 UK adults, about a quarter of the clothes people owned (26%, or 31 items on average) hadn't been worn for at least a year. Photographing those first is the slowest way to a useful app.

How to digitize your wardrobe, step by step

1. Set up one photo spot

Pick a place near a window and shoot in daylight with the room lights off. Indyx's photo guide points out that artificial light can change how an item's colour looks, and GetWardrobe's help pages advise against flash because it creates harsh shadows. Overcast daylight is ideal; direct sun throws hard shadows of its own.

For the background, use something plain that contrasts with the clothes: a bed sheet, a towel, a clean floor. A white shirt on a white sheet is hard for an app to cut out, so keep a dark surface for light pieces and a light one for dark pieces. Avoid strongly coloured backgrounds, which can reflect onto the fabric and throw the colour off.

Keep personal details out of the frame, especially if your app stores photos online: crop out faces in mirror shots, post with your address on it and anything else you wouldn't post publicly.

2. Lay each piece flat and shoot from above

Flat lays beat hangers, which pull garments out of shape in photos. Hold the phone parallel to the item, directly above it, so nothing looks stretched. A few habits make the photos far easier to use later:

  • Fasten buttons and zips, and lay shoulders straight.
  • Tuck sleeves along the sides instead of spreading them out.
  • Fill the frame without cutting off any part of the item.
  • Shoot shoes and structured bags from the side, toes all pointing the same way.
  • Wipe the lens first. A smudged lens softens every photo in the batch.

3. Shoot in a batch, upload in a batch

Photograph 15 or 20 pieces in one go, then add them from your camera roll together. It's much faster than switching between wardrobe and app for every item, and many apps accept several photos at once. GetWardrobe, for example, says its app takes up to 30 images at a time and removes backgrounds automatically. If your app doesn't remove backgrounds, the plain surface from step 1 does most of that job anyway.

4. Use shop photos only where they help

For something you bought recently and can still find online, a product photo saves time, and some apps can import an item straight from a shop link. Your own photo is still more honest: it shows the colour after twenty washes, not the colour in the studio. A mix is fine.

5. Tag with a handful of fields

Tags are what make the wardrobe searchable and what outfit suggestions are built from. Keep them short and consistent:

  • Type: shirt, jumper, jeans, trainers.
  • Main colour, and pattern if there is one (stripe, check, floral).
  • Season: warm weather, cold weather or all year.
  • Formality: casual, smart casual or formal.

That's enough for most people; GetWardrobe's guide also says category, colour and season are enough for good suggestions. Add price and purchase date only if your app tracks cost per wear and you'll look at it. Decide your words once: if one jumper is "navy", don't call the next one "dark blue".

Many apps now suggest tags automatically. Check each one, because colour shifts under warm light and formality is a judgement call. FitWardrobe, our app (it isn't available yet), is one example: AI tags each photo by type, colour, pattern, season and formality, and you can correct any tag.

6. Save the outfits you already wear

Before trying anything new, recreate five to ten outfits you already like and save them under the occasion they're for: office, weekend, dinner out. They're your baseline. After that, try one new combination a week and keep the ones that work.

7. Look at the whole wardrobe once

Scroll through everything you've added in one sitting. Seeing nine tops and two pairs of trousers side by side tells you more than any shopping list. Note what you notice, but don't shop yet; finish adding the clothes first.

What to skip

Leaving things out keeps the app quick to use. Most people can skip:

  • underwear, socks, pyjamas and basic gym kit, unless you plan those too
  • exact duplicates: photograph one of your five plain white T-shirts and add a note
  • anything you're about to give away or sell
  • out-of-season clothes in storage, until the season turns
  • detailed fields such as fabric, care instructions and brand, unless you'll actually use them

Do add the accessories that change an outfit: belts, scarves, bags and the hats you actually wear. Jewellery is optional.

How long it takes

It depends on how much you own and how you approach it. Three workable paces:

ApproachWhat it looks likeSuits
Starting set20 to 30 pieces in one evening, the rest added as you wear themMost people
A little each dayAround five items a day, which GetWardrobe's guide says gets you to 50 to 70 items in about two weeksLarge wardrobes, busy weeks
All at onceA weekend with everything out of the wardrobePeople who are decluttering anyway

The all-at-once approach is the easiest to abandon halfway, because it takes longest before the app is any use. If you choose it, pair it with a clear-out, so the photographing also decides what stays.

How to use an outfit app once your clothes are in

A catalogue earns its place when you start asking it questions. A few habits make an outfit app useful from the first week:

  1. Plan tomorrow tonight. Check the next day's plans and dress code, then build or request one complete outfit before you go to bed.
  2. Start from one piece. When you want to wear something specific, choose it first and build the rest of the outfit around it.
  3. Give feedback. Save the outfits you actually wear and dismiss the ones you wouldn't, if the app learns from that.
  4. Fix tags when a suggestion looks wrong. A shirt filed as a jacket or navy read as black is usually behind an odd pairing.

FitWardrobe, our outfit app, is built around that loop: pick an occasion or a piece and get an outfit from your own clothes with a line on why it works. It isn't available yet.

Keeping your digital wardrobe up to date

A digital wardrobe is only useful while it matches the real one. Four habits keep it that way:

  1. Photograph new clothes before the first wear, while they're clean and still folded.
  2. Use laundry day as a check. Anything you fold that isn't in the app gets photographed there and then.
  3. Delete or archive items the day they leave: given away, sold or worn out.
  4. Review at each season change. Fix tags, archive what's going into storage and bring back what's coming out.

Once it's current, the app starts paying back the setup time. Use it to plan outfits for the week on Sunday, or to lay out a travel capsule before you pack instead of emptying the wardrobe onto the bed.

faq.q: Is there an app for putting outfits together?
faq.a: Yes. Wardrobe apps, also called digital closet or outfit planner apps, let you photograph your clothes and combine them into outfits on screen. Some also suggest outfits from what you own. They differ in platform, price model and whether your photos are stored on your phone or online, so check those three things on the official store listing before you spend an evening adding clothes.

faq.q: How do I photograph clothes for a wardrobe app?
faq.a: Lay each piece flat on a plain background that contrasts with it, such as a dark sheet for light clothes, and shoot from directly above in daylight with the room lights and flash off. Fasten buttons, straighten the shoulders and tuck sleeves to the sides. Shoot shoes and structured bags from the side. Photograph a batch, then upload them together.

faq.q: Do I need to photograph every item I own?
faq.a: No. Start with the 20 to 30 pieces you've worn in the last month or two, plus shoes and outerwear, and add the rest as you wear them. Skip underwear, socks, exact duplicates and anything you're about to give away. A UK survey by WRAP found about a quarter of people's clothes hadn't been worn in a year, so those can wait.

faq.q: How long does it take to digitize a wardrobe?
faq.a: It depends on how much you own and your approach. A starting set of 20 to 30 pieces fits into one evening if you photograph in a batch. Adding about five items a day gets you to 50 to 70 pieces in about two weeks. Doing everything in one weekend is possible but tiring, and works best if you're decluttering at the same time.

faq.q: Can I use photos from online shops instead of my own?
faq.a: Yes, for items you can still find online, and some apps can import an item from a shop link. Product photos look neat but show the colour from the studio, not after months of washing, so your own photo is usually more accurate for colour matching. A mix works well: shop images for recent purchases, your own photos for everything else.

faq.q: How do I keep a digital wardrobe up to date?
faq.a: Build it into routines you already have. Photograph new clothes before their first wear, check for missing items on laundry day, and delete or archive pieces the day you give them away. At each change of season, fix any wrong tags and archive what's going into storage. A digital wardrobe that drifts from the real one quickly stops being useful.
